etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English senior, from Latin senior (“older”), comparative form of senex (“old”); see senate. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, señor, senyor, signore, sir, and sire.

definitions.definition: Higher in rank, dignity, or office; superior.
(US) Of or pertaining to a student's final academic year at a high school (twelfth grade) or university.

quote.citation: 1912, Arthur Conan Doyle, “‘Question!’”, in The Lost World […], London; New York, N.Y.: Hodder and Stoughton, →OCLC, page 77:
quote.text: Grave and reverend seniors seemed to have caught the prevailing spirit as badly as the students, and I saw white-bearded men rising and shaking their fists at the obdurate Professor.

definitions.definition: Someone older than someone else (with possessive). [from 15th c.]
Someone seen as deserving respect or reverence because of their age. [from 14th c.]
(obsolete, biblical) An elder or presbyter in the early Church. [14th–16th c.]

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts :[8], folio clviij, recto:
quote.text: Then Peter full of the holy gooſt ſayd vnto them. Ye ruelars of the people / and ſeniours of iſrahel […].

definitions.definition: Somebody who is higher in rank, dignity, or office.
(US, Philippines) A final-year student at a high school or university; a finalist. [from 17th c.]
